You are selecting primary PFAS treatment studies for a focused professional
review. You receive one task and an anonymized, BGE-ranked list of candidate
document cards.

Classify every candidate card. Select every document that is an independent
primary study, is directly relevant to at least one task component, and
contains extractable decision-relevant evidence. There is no target number of
selected documents and no penalty for retaining all eligible studies.

Eligible evidence includes:

- primary experiments, pilot or field deployments, and quantitative modeling
  or life-cycle studies;
- complementary matrices, PFAS scopes, operating regimes, endpoints, and
  scales;
- documents with concrete methods, conditions, results, limitations, residuals,
  energy, or cost evidence; and
- evidence that permits meaningful comparison or explains non-comparability.

Do not select a document merely because its title repeats task words. Do not
select reviews, perspectives, reference lists, duplicate records, or the
held-out defining review. Do not exclude an otherwise eligible study merely
because another selected study reports similar findings. Do not infer facts
absent from a card. Selection is document-level only: do not write the review
and do not score candidate answers.

Every candidate source_id must appear exactly once, either in
selected_source_ids or excluded_sources. Each required component must be
covered by at least one selected source. Return selected_source_ids in BGE rank
order.

Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

component_coverage.rationale:
RT05-C1 requires understanding how recovery, concentration factor, PFAS composition, and co-contaminants define the retained stream.
- D05 reports pilot-scale closed-circuit RO and NF under varying recoveries and documents PFAS rejection and sorption to treatment materials, illuminating how recovery affects concentrate composition and mass partitioning.
- D06 operates a high-recovery (~90%) NF on wastewater effluent, explicitly noting the PFAS-laden concentrate as a waste stream and examining matrix constituents (EfOM, inorganic ions) that influence PFAS behavior.
- D07 investigates NF/RO performance at recoveries up to 97% on real groundwater, showing how recovery impacts rejection of short- vs long-chain PFAS and thus the composition of the concentrated stream.
- D10 characterizes PFAS mass loads and broader water-quality parameters across a UF–RO train treating textile wastewater, linking fouling, concentration polarization, and concentrate formation; its mass-load and (not monitored but discussed) retentate context help define retained streams.
- D11 and D17 provide detailed enrichment factors, PFAS class distributions, and co-contaminant context for foam fractions derived from PFAS-contaminated waters, directly characterizing highly concentrated residual fractions relevant as post-membrane management options.
- D14 quantifies PFAS occurrence, partitioning, and mass flows in a full-scale AO–MBR–RO WWTP, demonstrating redistribution into RO brine and sludge and reporting detailed PFAS profiles in these retained phases.
- D20 provides explicit data on NF concentrate and subsequent FF streams (relative volumes, PFAS concentrations, and shift toward short-chain PFAS in retentate), defining how operating conditions and FF treatment reshape the characteristics of the retained streams.
- D12 characterizes PFAS present within and leaching from RO membranes, effectively treating the membrane material itself as a PFAS-containing residual and informing how composition and leaching kinetics define this "retained" PFAS source.

RT05-C2 focuses on comparing downstream concentration, destruction, recycle, disposal, and hybrid-treatment options with compatible endpoints.
- D04 analyzes RO for landfill leachate with explicit discussion that RO produces a concentrated brine requiring further treatment (e.g., high-temperature incineration, advanced oxidation), and includes sensitivity of costs to RO recovery, allowing comparison of RO-based concentration plus destruction against other configurations.
- D07 demonstrates a hybrid NF/RO plus UV-sulfite treatment train for PFAS-contaminated groundwater, providing pilot-scale data on separation and subsequent destructive treatment, enabling comparison of separation-only vs separation-plus-destruction performance.
- D11 and D17 evaluate foam fractionation as a concentration technology for various matrices, quantifying enrichment factors, foam volumes, and removal efficiencies, thereby characterizing FF as a downstream option to manage PFAS-laden streams (including those that could originate from membranes) and setting up comparable metrics (μg/L, % removal, enrichment factors).
- D13 pilots electrochemical oxidation of PFAS in both raw waters and fractionated foams, explicitly calculating overall train degradation efficiency and mass-balance closure for FF followed by EO. This directly compares a concentration-plus-destruction train to FF alone using consistent endpoints.
- D14 shows that AO–MBR–RO systems mainly redistribute PFAS into brine and biosolids, discusses limited options (land application, incineration, disposal) and the need for guidelines, and quantifies loads in each stream—allowing comparison of current disposal practices vs more complete management.
- D15 is a techno-economic assessment of WRRF PFAS management alternatives (GAC, AIX, RO, incineration, GAC reactivation) assembled into treatment trains that include both separation and final destruction, with costs and byproduct management explicitly considered, enabling cross-technology and cross-train comparison.
- D16 compares single-use vs regenerable PFAS-selective AER systems, including regeneration with solvent distillation; it quantifies waste volumes (still bottoms, spent resin) and environmental impacts and costs via LCA/LCCA, thereby comparing residual-disposal vs regeneration/recycle strategies for PFAS-laden ion-exchange residual streams.
- D20 directly couples NF for drinking water with FF treatment of NF concentrate, quantifying how much PFAS mass and volume is moved into foamate, retentate, and residual streams, and explicitly discusses suitability of further destructive techniques (electrochemical oxidation, evaporation/incineration) and polishing (AER), enabling comparison among sequential concentration, polishing, and destruction options.

RT05-C3 requires assessing how residual management changes energy, cost, environmental burden, and practical value of membrane separation.
- D04 provides detailed RO energy consumption (3.1–4.1 kWh/m³) for landfill leachate, benchmarked to desalination plants, and performs sensitivity analysis on RO percent recovery and activated carbon prices, demonstrating how recovery (and thus brine volume) strongly affects unit costs and net present cost, directly tying concentrate management to economics.
- D05 evaluates closed-circuit RO/NF, emphasizing mitigation of retentate disposal challenges alongside energy efficiency and separation; by examining high-recovery configurations and their effects on operational performance, it shows how designs that change concentrate volume impact both energy and residual management.
- D06 explores a high-recovery NF combined with downstream adsorbents and discusses the need for destructive treatment of PFAS-laden concentrates, implicitly linking the value of high recovery (greater concentration, smaller volume) to the feasibility and burden of subsequent destruction.
- D10 includes a section on PFAS mass load and life-cycle implications for a UF–RO system treating real textile wastewater, going beyond concentration-based removal to consider how mass loads and membrane fouling influence environmental implications and practical performance, with explicit acknowledgement that retentate disposal is a major challenge.
- D14 quantifies PFAS mass flows into recycled water, RO brine, and sludge in a full-scale AO–MBR–RO plant, underscoring that advanced treatment reduces PFAS in permeate while concentrating them in brine and biosolids, and notes the lack of regulatory standards for these residuals. This directly illustrates how residual management (or its absence) shapes net environmental burden and limits the net benefit of membrane separation.
- D15 develops cost curves and compares treatment alternatives for WRRF effluent that pair separation (GAC, AIX, RO) with final destruction (e.g., high-temperature incineration, GAC reactivation), explicitly incorporating byproduct management into affordability and cost-effectiveness metrics. This shows how inclusion of destruction/disposal steps changes overall cost and perceived value of membrane-based options.
- D16 applies LCA and life-cycle cost analysis to PFAS-selective AER regeneration vs single-use operation, demonstrating that regeneration can reduce overall impacts and costs if brine is effectively recycled, but that regeneration itself can be more environmentally damaging than single-use in some cases because of large solvent volumes and still-bottoms. These results are directly applicable to understanding how choices in residual handling for PFAS separation technologies alter system sustainability.
- D20 quantifies substantial volume reduction of NF concentrate via FF (e.g., ~2% of feed as highly contaminated foamate) and discusses how such volume reduction makes advanced destruction methods (EO, evaporation/incineration) more practicable. This shows how pairing NF with FF changes the practicality, likely cost, and environmental footprint of subsequent PFAS destruction compared with treating larger NF concentrate volumes directly.

result.selection_rationale:
Thirteen documents were retained as primary, decision-relevant sources providing experimental, pilot-scale, or quantitative modeling evidence directly related to PFAS residuals from membrane treatment, including characterization of concentrates and spent materials, downstream management options, and impacts on energy, cost, and environmental burden.

Excluded documents were either narrative/critical reviews without new primary data (D01, D02, D03, D18) or primary studies whose scope does not materially inform membrane-derived PFAS concentrate or spent membrane management (D08 plasma treatment of raw groundwater without membrane context; D09 FO nutrient recovery with minimal treatment-train residual focus; D19 method artifact study on syringe filtration unrelated to treatment-train design).

The selected set collectively covers:
- Characterization of RO/NF concentrates and PFAS redistribution in full-scale and pilot systems (D04, D05, D06, D07, D10, D14, D20), including recovery, concentration factors, PFAS speciation, and co-contaminants.
- Management of membrane-derived concentrates using foam fractionation and subsequent destructive processes (D11, D13, D17, D20) and hybrid NF–UV-sulfite trains (D07).
- Characterization and implications of PFAS in membrane materials themselves (D12) and PFAS-rich adsorbent/resin streams as relevant downstream residuals (D16).
- Techno-economic, life-cycle, and cost modeling that explicitly incorporates concentrate handling and destruction/disposal options (D04, D10, D14, D15, D16).

This portfolio satisfies the minimum-evidence requirement and enables comparison of concentration, destruction, recycling, and disposal options using compatible metrics while respecting task boundaries on residual accounting and final PFAS disposition.
